title: JUST TWO MINUTES.
narration: It's eleven forty-two. Alex gets into bed and opens a feed. Just two minutes. A funny dog. A cooking trick. Someone explaining why everyone else is wrong. One more swipe.

title: HOW IS IT ALREADY 12:26?
narration: Now it's twelve twenty-six. Alex isn't even having much fun anymore. But the thumb is still moving. How does something you barely enjoy become so hard to put down?

title: WANTING MORE ≠ ENJOYING THIS
narration: Part of the answer is that wanting to check the next thing and enjoying the thing in front of you are different experiences. A feed can keep inviting the first without delivering much of the second.

title: A LONG SESSION CAN BE A GOOD SESSION
narration: That doesn't make every long session a problem. Watching a concert you love, learning a skill, or talking with a friend can be time well spent. The question is whether you're still doing what you meant to do.

title: IT CAN START BEFORE YOU DECIDE
narration: Sometimes a notification starts it. Sometimes it's just a familiar moment: waiting for coffee, finishing a task, or lying in bed. Your hand reaches for the phone before you've named a reason.

title: A SMALL CHECK CAN BECOME A SESSION
narration: Researchers studying smartphone use have described checking habits: brief, repeated visits to changing content. Those checks can lead into other activities on the device. A quick look doesn't always stay quick.

title: CUE → OPEN → SWIPE → REPEAT
narration: For Alex, the sequence is familiar. Feel a little bored. Open the app. Swipe. Something changes immediately. After enough repetition in the same setting, the sequence can start feeling automatic.

title: SOME EXPERIENCES COME WITH AN END
narration: A chapter ends. The credits roll. A friend says goodbye. Those moments give you an obvious chance to decide what happens next. An endless feed makes that pause much less obvious.

title: THE NEXT ITEM IS ALREADY THERE
narration: There isn't necessarily a last page waiting below your thumb. More content loads as you move. You don't have to make a fresh decision to start another session. Continuing is the easy default.

title: ONE LESS MOMENT TO CHOOSE
narration: Autoplay can remove another decision. The next clip starts before you've really asked whether you want it. Each transition is tiny. Added together, they can carry you beyond your original plan.

title: MAYBE THE NEXT ONE WILL BE BETTER
narration: And the next item is uncertain. Some posts are boring. Some are funny. Some feel strangely relevant. Even when this one disappoints, the possibility that the next one will be better can keep the search going.

title: A PROMISE ISN’T THE SAME AS A PAYOFF
narration: Notice the bargain Alex keeps making. Not, this is great. More like, maybe something great is one swipe away. That's a useful way to describe the experience, not a measurement of anyone's brain chemistry.

title: REWARDS CAN SHAPE WHAT WE DO
narration: Research has found that social rewards, like likes, can influence posting behavior. That's evidence about reward learning in a particular setting. It doesn't prove that every swipe, every app, or every person works the same way.

title: WHAT WAS ALEX LOOKING FOR?
narration: Tonight, Alex was also looking for a break from tomorrow's to-do list. The feed briefly gives that attention somewhere else to go. But a break that keeps extending can stop being the break Alex actually wanted.

title: THE CLOCK FALLS OUT OF THE PICTURE
narration: Another part of the experience is absorption. You can become so focused on the next item that the room, the clock, and your original intention fade into the background. You may only notice afterward.

title: INTERFACE DESIGN CAN MAKE A DIFFERENCE
narration: In one study, forty-three people used a custom social media app. Features including reading-history labels and time reminders reduced self-reported absorption of this kind. That was one study in one app, not a universal cure.

title: A SWIPE ISN’T A BRAIN SCAN
narration: So this isn't a diagnosis, and a long scrolling session doesn't tell us your dopamine level. Habit, design, context, and what you're looking for can all matter. The explanation needs more than a single chemical.

title: GIVE THE DECISION A PLACE TO HAPPEN
narration: What can Alex change? Start by making a stopping moment visible. Before opening the feed, decide what this visit is for, and what will tell you it's finished.

title: “I’M HERE TO WATCH THREE SAVED CLIPS.”
narration: Maybe the plan is three saved clips. Maybe it's ten minutes, followed by putting the phone on the shelf. The exact number isn't magic. What matters is choosing an ending before the feed chooses another beginning.

title: PUT THE REMINDER OUTSIDE THE FEED
narration: An outside cue can make that ending easier to notice. Alex uses a small timer across the room. When it rings, the next step is physical: stand up, then decide whether to return.

title: TRY A FINITE LIST
narration: A saved list or a specific search can also give a visit a shape. Find the recipe. Watch the three clips. Send the message. Then let finishing that task count as a real ending.

title: MAKE THE AUTOMATIC STEP LESS AUTOMATIC
narration: You can also add a little friction: move the app off the first screen, turn off nonessential notifications, or disable autoplay where the app allows it. Treat these as experiments, not guarantees.

title: HELPFUL FRICTION CAN STILL BE ANNOYING
narration: There's a tradeoff. In a small experiment, requiring people to react before seeing another post improved content recognition, but many found it frustrating. A useful boundary should help you choose without making your whole phone miserable.

title: GIVE THE PHONE A PARKING SPOT
narration: For Alex, another experiment is simply charging the phone away from the bed. That changes the familiar setup. The phone is still available; reaching for it now involves a more deliberate action.

title: WHAT KIND OF BREAK DO YOU WANT?
narration: It helps to have an actual next activity. A glass of water. A few pages of a book. Sleep. Or even a deliberately chosen video. Closing a feed is easier to plan when there's something concrete on the other side.

title: ONE CHANGE. ONE WEEK. NOTICE THE DIFFERENCE.
narration: You don't have to change everything tonight. Pick one boundary and try it for a week. Ask whether it helped you notice the decision point, and whether the time you spent felt worthwhile.

title: THIS TIME, THE TIMER GETS A SAY
narration: The next night, Alex opens the feed again. The timer rings. There's still another interesting clip waiting. But now there's also a clear moment to ask: do I actually want to keep going?

title: CONTINUING CAN BE A CHOICE, TOO
narration: Sometimes the answer will be yes. That's fine. The goal isn't to make every minute productive, or to feel guilty about entertainment. It's to make continuing a choice you recognize making.

title: TWO MINUTES DOESN’T HAVE TO BECOME AN HOUR
narration: Tonight, Alex puts the phone on the shelf. Tomorrow might be messier. A habit doesn't disappear because you understood one explanation. But the next attempt can begin with a better setup, rather than another argument with yourself.

title: IS THIS STILL WHAT I CHOSE TO DO?
narration: The next time your thumb keeps moving after the fun has faded, try a different question. Not just, what's next? Ask: is this still what I chose to do? Give yourself a moment to answer.
